name: Pedro Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Castell Building Supplies, a distributor that sells timber, plasterboard, cement and fixings to builders' merchants. I'm the junior buyer, so I do the screws, nails and fixings, which is about four hundred product lines. Most of my day is the phone and a big spreadsheet my old manager built, checking what's low and ringing the suppliers. I like the suppliers, they're good people, and I don't like the head office emails telling us to try new systems.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of new systems do they send?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last year it was an ordering portal and this year it's some AI assistant they want us to try. I haven't touched it. My spreadsheet works, I know where everything is, and I'm still slow enough at the job without learning another thing. I'm on lower pay than the other buyers and my girlfriend Ana and I have maybe a few weeks of money saved, so I keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, it was mostly talk. I'm not one for posting, but I'd say it at the canteen. People got worked up about nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but I'd still worry a bit. Even if AI just does routine tasks, my job is quite a lot of routine tasks, like keying orders in. If head office makes the portal do that, my manager might wonder what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it. Maybe I'd learn the ordering portal properly, just the basics, so nobody can say I'm behind. And I'd keep putting a bit by each month, even if it's just thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. There's still that small knot about money, but that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money knot about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana's a hairdresser and some weeks are quiet. Our car needs a new clutch, which is about six hundred, and we haven't got that sitting around. We'll put it on the card, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Castell would you talk to if you got worried about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Steve in the yard, he's been there twenty years. He'd tell me straight. My manager is nice but she's very head office.

say: I'd say at the canteen that AI was **mostly talk** and people got worked up.
I wouldn't post online; I'm **not one** for that.
think: My job is a lot of **routine keying**, so even small automation could touch it.
If the **portal** does my orders, my manager might wonder what I'm for.
do: Keep doing the job with **my spreadsheet**.
Learn the **ordering portal** basics so nobody says I'm behind.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a small **knot** about money that never goes.
S0.quote: Even if AI just does routine tasks, my job is quite a lot of routine tasks, like keying orders in.
fieldNote: Pedro has **never used** AI tools and relies on a spreadsheet he inherited.
He sees even mild automation touching his **routine order entry**.
His money worry is real but **everyday**: a six-hundred clutch on the card.

steps.text: Keep ordering fixings from his own spreadsheet
Learn the basics of the head office ordering portal
Put thirty a month aside for repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will always look for savings. I wouldn't be angry online, there's no point. At work I'd keep quiet and do my job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be the first to go and I know it. I'm junior, I'm not the best buyer, and I'm the one who won't use the AI. If head office says one buyer can do the work of two with this software, it's not going to be the guy with the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my uncle Luis, who has a tiling business, and ask if he'd take me on if it came to that. I'd probably force myself to try the assistant, even if I hate it, just so they see me using it. And Ana and I would stop eating out and stop the holiday fund, which is only small anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. My stomach turns. I don't like change, and this is change aimed right at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to actually open the AI assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager standing behind me, honestly. I know that sounds stubborn. I just feel stupid using it, like it knows more about my job than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you went to your uncle's, what would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The suppliers. I've got a rep, Gary, who rings me every Tuesday and we talk football for ten minutes before prices. Tiling is just you and a wall.

say: I'd say it's just **business**; companies always look for savings.
At work I'd **keep quiet** and do the job well instead of complaining.
think: I'm junior, not the best, and the **one who won't** use the AI.
If one buyer can do two buyers' work, they'll keep the one with the **software**.
do: Ask Uncle Luis about working in his **tiling business**.
Force myself to **try the assistant** so managers see it.
Stop eating out and pause the **holiday fund**.
feel: **Bad**, with a turning stomach at change aimed **right at me**.
S1.quote: If head office says one buyer can do the work of two with this software, it's not going to be the guy with the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Pedro expects to be **first out** and says so plainly.
He feels **stupid** using AI, which keeps him from the one thing that might help.
His backup is **family**: his uncle's tiling firm, hands-on and later to automate.

steps.text: Ask Uncle Luis for a job in his tiling business
Open head office's AI assistant and use it for orders
Stop eating out and pause the holiday fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what anyone can do about that. Maybe that the government has to sort something out. I'd say it quietly, I'm not a protest guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm gone in a year, not two. Buying is all thinking work, and I'm already behind. The only good part is that tiling and building are hands-on, so if I get into my uncle's firm I've got until about 2031 before robots do walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Luis straight away and start working Saturdays for him, to learn. I'd leave Castell the moment he could pay me full time, even for less. Ana and I would give up the flat and move in with her parents, who have a spare room. We'd sell the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I wouldn't sleep. I like knowing what next year looks like, and with AGI in two years I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's just for a while. Her dad would be fine, he likes me, but her mum would worry about us not getting married and living in her house. That conversation would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come for tiling around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no idea. I'd be thirty-two. I'd just hope someone has a plan, because I won't.

say: I'd say quietly that the **government** has to sort something out.
I'd admit I **don't know** what anyone could do about it.
think: I'm gone in **a year**, because buying is all thinking work and I'm behind.
Tiling is **hands-on**, so I'd have until about 2031 before robots.
do: Work **Saturdays** for Luis now and leave Castell when he can pay me.
Give up the flat and **move in** with Ana's parents.
feel: **Frightened** and sleepless, with no idea what **next year** looks like.
S2.quote: I like knowing what next year looks like, and with AGI in two years I wouldn't.
fieldNote: Pedro has **no plan** past the robot date and says he won't have one.
He grabs the **family route** into tiling as the only shelter.
Moving in with Ana's parents brings a **family tension** he dreads.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at Uncle Luis's tiling firm to learn the trade
Give up the flat and move into Ana's parents' spare room
Lean on Ana's parents for a home while money is short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still fast, but at least people can plan. Probably that firms like Castell should help staff find something else. I'd say that to the manager if she asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably waste the first two years hoping it doesn't happen. That's what I'm like. But I know the buying goes by 2031, and tiling would last until 2034, so I'd have to make the move at some point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep my job and do Saturdays with Luis, so I learn without giving anything up. I'd try to save a bit from the Saturday money, maybe a hundred a month. Maybe I'd use the AI assistant at work, just enough to stay off the list for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a dentist appointment I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first two years. Why tell me that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's true. I wait for things until I have to move. With five years I'd tell myself there's plenty of time, until there isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Castell didn't replace someone who left, or if Steve in the yard said it's time. I trust him more than the emails.

say: I'd say five years is fast, but at least people **can plan**.
I'd tell my manager firms should **help staff** find something else.
think: I'd probably **waste two years** hoping it doesn't happen.
Buying goes by **2031** and tiling lasts until 2034, so I must move sometime.
do: Keep the Castell job and do **Saturdays** with Luis.
Save about **a hundred** a month from the Saturday money.
Use the **AI assistant** just enough to stay off the list.
feel: **Uneasy** all the time, like a **dentist appointment** I keep moving.
S3.quote: I wait for things until I have to move. With five years I'd tell myself there's plenty of time, until there isn't.
fieldNote: Pedro is **honest about delay**, admitting he'd waste the early years.
He keeps his job and builds a **tiling skill** on the side without risk.
His trusted signal is **Steve in the yard**, not head office.

steps.text: Keep the Castell job while waiting for clear signs
Work Saturdays tiling for Uncle Luis
Save a hundred a month from Saturday pay
Use the AI assistant enough to stay off the cut list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change. I'd tell people not to panic. At work I'd probably say I'll worry about it in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the first one where I think I'd be alright. I could learn tiling slowly with Luis, maybe take over some of his jobs when he slows down, and stay at Castell for a few more years first. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, still young enough for a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd just keep going at Castell and maybe ask Luis about one Saturday a month. I'd start saving properly, because Ana wants to get married and that costs. I wouldn't touch the AI unless they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit worried, but it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still not use the AI, even with ten years warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not until I have to. I know that's not smart. I'd rather put the hours into tiling, which I can see with my own eyes, than into an AI I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still do it, just small, maybe at her parents' church hall. Ten years is enough time to get married and still sort out work.

say: I'd tell people **not to panic**, since ten years is a long time.
At work I'd joke that I'll worry about it in **2035**.
think: Ten years is the first picture where I'd likely be **alright**.
I could learn tiling slowly and maybe **take over** some of Luis's jobs later.
do: Keep working at **Castell** and do one Saturday a month with Luis.
Start saving properly for a **small wedding**.
Avoid the **AI assistant** unless head office makes it compulsory.
feel: **Calmer**, with a little worry that still feels far away.
S4.quote: I'd rather put the hours into tiling, which I can see with my own eyes, than into an AI I don't trust.
fieldNote: Even with ten years Pedro **won't use AI** voluntarily; his resistance is firm.
His job still ends, so worry stays, but the **tiling route** feels realistic.
Life plans continue: a **small wedding** with Ana stays on.

steps.text: Keep buying fixings at Castell for now
Do one Saturday a month tiling with Uncle Luis
Plan a small wedding at Ana's parents' church hall
Save each month for the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough for someone like me, who takes ages to change. What would help is something that keeps the rent paid while I learn a trade, and maybe the company giving us a year's notice instead of a month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're good at that isn't on a screen. I know four hundred fixings and which supplier lies about delivery dates. Nobody asks if that's worth anything somewhere else.

headlineQuote: I know four hundred fixings and which supplier lies about delivery dates. Nobody asks if that's worth anything somewhere else.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** junior buyer of screws and fixings at a building supplies distributor.
He runs his work from an **inherited spreadsheet** and has never used the AI assistant head office pushes.
He and girlfriend Ana, a hairdresser, have **a few weeks** of savings and a car needing repairs.
He expects to be **first out** in most pictures, and his backup is his uncle's **tiling** firm.
He admits he waits until forced to move, so even ten years leaves him **anxious**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone who changes slowly.
whatWouldHelp: Something to keep the **rent paid** while learning a trade, and a **year's notice** from employers.
